                                          PROJECT NO. 58481

 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                                 §              BEFORE THE
 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                              §      PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA 37.0561                            §               OF TEXAS

                                   CLOUDHQ, LLC'S COMMENTS

        On March 16, 2026, the Public Utility Commission of Texas ("PUCT" or "Commission")
published its "(Staff Recommendation) Proposal for Publication" relating to Large Load
Interconnection Standards, 16 Texas Administrative Code (TAC) § 25.194 (the "Proposed
Interconnection Rules"), as mandated by Public Utility Regulatory Act (PURA) § 37.0561,
enacted by Senate Bill (SB) 6 during the Texas 89th Regular Legislative Session ("SB 6"). In
publishing the Proposed Interconnection Rules, the Commission specifically requested comments
on the proposed rules, including "the costs associated with, and benefits that will be gained by,
implementation of the proposed rule." In response to the Commission's request for comments,
CloudHQ LLC ("CloudHQ") herein provides its comments and proposed revisions to the Proposed
Interconnection Rules.
I.      ABOUT CLOUDHQ

        CloudHQ1 is global data center company that partners with the world's largest technology
companies to provide reliable and secure power and operating infrastructure. Since its founding in
2016, CloudHQ and its affiliates have successfully leased data centers totaling 1,380 megawatts
("MWs") of capacity across 24 campuses around the globe, with projects in the United States,
United Kingdom, European Union, Asia-Pacific, Central America, and South America. Presently,
CloudHQ is actively pursuing the development of an additional 5 GW of capacity across the globe,
including a ~500 MW data center that it is currently developing west of San Antonio on the former
University of Texas Health Science Center site.2
        This background is provided so that the Commission understands that CloudHQ's interest
in this proceeding is neither theoretical nor speculative. CloudHQ is actively developing a data
center in Texas, and the decisions made via this rulemaking may determine whether CloudHQ can


        1
            References in this submission to CloudHQ refer to CloudHQ LLC and the affiliates under the common
control of CloudHQ's founder and CEO, Hossein Fateh.
        2
            https://cloudhq.com/campus/sat-campus/



                                                     1
 continue to undertake the risks of developing future data center projects, or whether the rules will
make such development impractical.
II.    INTRODUCTION

       With an ERCOT interconnection queue that has ballooned to 410 GW as of April 1, 2026,3
CloudHQ recognizes–and strongly supports the conclusion–that something must be done to ensure
that (1) the load seeking interconnection is real and not speculative; and (2) that any new load pays
its fair share. CloudHQ is fully supportive of requiring large load customers to make up-front
financial commitments as a pre-condition to interconnecting in the State. At the same time,
interconnecting should not become so onerous, expensive, and punitive that it disincentivizes (if
not eviscerates) large load investment and business development in the State.
       Fundamentally, CloudHQ believes that SB 6 properly sought to address the problems
facing ERCOT without stopping all large load growth in Texas. Unlike SB 6, however, CloudHQ
does not believe that the Proposed Interconnection Rules adequately balance these interests,
however, it is critical that this balance is reflected in the final version of these rules because SB 6
demands it. Specifically, SB 6 obligates the Commission to
       establish standards for interconnecting large load customers in the ERCOT power
       region in a manner designed to support business development in this state while
       minimizing the potential for stranded infrastructure costs and maintaining system
       reliability.4

The Commission was directed to establish interconnection rules that are designed to support
business development while mitigating the risks of stranded costs and maintaining system
reliability. The Proposed Interconnection Rules fail to achieve the balance explicitly set forth in
SB 6. As written, the Proposed Interconnection Rules focus solely on eliminating (rather than
mitigating) customer risk, and rather than taking steps to ensure that business development will be
supported, they instead go the opposite direction, unduly restricting future large, grid connected,
load. Without changes, the Proposed Interconnection Rules have the potential to significantly stifle
business development and growth in Texas.




       3
            Pablo Vegas, ERCOT Update–Senate Committee on Business & Commerce (April 1, 2026),
https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2026/04/01/ERCOT_LargeLoad_Update_April2026_B-C_-Hearing.pdf
       4
           PURA § 37.0561(b) (emphasis added).



                                                  2
 III.   COMMENTS

       A.        The Commission Should Strike Section (h) from the Final Rule.

       From CloudHQ's perspective, the single most problematic provision of the Proposed
Interconnection Rules is set forth in Section (h)(1), (6) where it states in relevant part:
       Not later than 30 days after a large load customer fails, by 6 months, to satisfy a
       milestone in its schedule for phased energization, the interconnecting DSP or the
       interconnecting TSP must notify ERCOT of the large load customer's non-utilized
       capacity . . . [and] ERCOT must reallocate non-utilized capacity.5

This provision is unjust, unreasonable, vague, and unnecessary, and it should be stricken from the
Proposed Interconnection Rules in its entirety.
       The fundamental problem currently facing the Texas grid is not whether interconnected
load will use power once interconnected and operational. The real problems are in (1) determining
how much of the 410 GW in the queue is real and (2) in interconnecting such load, ensuring that
this new load–rather than existing customers–pay for the costs they cause. In proposing to take
away capacity from a customer that has already connected to the grid and paid substantial costs to
be interconnected, Section (h)(1) unjustly and unreasonably punishes large loads who legitimately
want to do business in Texas while not solving the fundamental issues facing the Texas grid.
       Not only is Section (h) unnecessary, but it unfairly vague. It is unclear what "milestone"
means within the context of Section (h) as it is undefined. Further, while Section (h)(1) discusses
a "large load customer" who "fails…to satisfy a milestone," there is no explanation of how to
determine whether a failed milestone is material, let alone whether the missed milestone is the
customer's fault as opposed to the fault of the transmission service provider ("TSP"), the
distribution service provider ("DSP"), ERCOT, or some other party.
       Section (h)(1) is also fundamentally unfair. While a TSP and DSP appear to be given carte
blanche to unilaterally determine that a milestone has been missed by a customer, there is no
process in place for a customer to challenge a determination by a TSP or DSP that a customer
failure has occurred so as to trigger ERCOT's reallocation of the capacity. Quite simply,
Section (h) of the Proposed Interconnection Rules could leave a customer who has expended
millions, if not billions of dollars, in capital, at risk of losing contracted–and paid–for capacity


       5
           Id.



                                                   3
 with no remedy simply because it missed some unknown and undefined milestone by six
(6) months and one (1) day.
        Most importantly, the provision places an immense amount of unnecessary risk on any new
large, grid connected, load in Texas that has already shown a commitment to locating–and
operating–in Texas. Indeed, at the time Section (h)(1) attaches, a data center customer will have
already spent millions (if not billions) of dollars on top of those required by the Proposed
Interconnection Rules to secure a site and necessary permits and construct the data center. Indeed,
at least one 2025 study suggests that the average costs of data center construction in Texas is
$11.7 million per MW,6 before accounting for the costs of servers, which are often the highest cost
incurred by data centers. To put this in perspective, a theoretical 200 MW data center project may
deploy approximately $2 billion of capital to construct a data center project, not including land
acquisition costs or the costs of the servers. However, if a large load customer fails to satisfy a
milestone in its schedule for phased energization by six months and one day, the large load
customer risks being left with nothing but a stranded asset without power, putting potentially
billions of dollars of investment at risk. This is a risk that few, if any, data center developers, chip
fabrication facilities, or other large industrial customers could bear. The consequences of this
punitive language not only run counter to the supportive business development envisioned by
SB 6, but it may also significantly stifle future business expansion and large-scale, grid-
interconnected, load-driven economic growth in Texas.
        Even if the Commission could fix the vagueness of undefined terms, clarify customer fault,
and provide a fair dispute resolution mechanism, this all begs the question: why is this provision
even needed? Under the Proposed Interconnection Rules, a customer governed by Section (h)
would have already signed an interconnection agreement, and, assuming the rules are implemented
as written, the customer would have:
        1. Paid $50,000/MW, which is non-refundable pursuant to Section (f)(7);
        2. Posted security for any "significant equipment or services" that are needed in order to
            "interconnect the large load customer" as required by Section (f)(8);
        3. Paid all costs deemed Contribution in Aid of Construction ("CIAC"), none of which
            are subject to refund as set forth in Section (f)(9); and

          6
                  Data Center Development Cost Guide 2025, Cushman & Wakefield, at 9,
https://digital.cushmanwakefield.com/Data-Center-Development-Cost-Guide-2025/8-9/ (last visited Apr. 14, 2026).



                                                      4
         4. Posted security for system upgrades necessary to serve that customer as required by
              Section (f)(10).
        It is also important to remember that the financial security under the Proposed
Interconnection Rules are not the only forms of security being considered by this Commission. In
Project No. 58484, the Commission is currently assessing the methodology for allocating
transmission costs to the DSP and the appropriate customer class.7 Among the proposals being
considered by the Commission are minimum demand charges based on a large load customer's
contracted peak demand. A minimum demand charge is a better approach for ensuring that
contracted for capacity is utilized by a large load customer; not only does it protect other
customers, but it does so in a manner that is less problematic than Section (h)(1) of these Proposed
Interconnection Rules.
        Section (h)(1) is not an appropriate solution for the problems facing the Texas grid. As
proposed, it serves as a punitive and fundamentally unfair measure to large load customers that
also fails to achieve the balance inherent in SB 6. As reflected above, there are other, better
mechanisms available, some of which are included in the Proposed Interconnection Rules, to
ensure that customers are protected and assets are not stranded. There is no justifiable reason to
reallocate a customer's capacity as proposed in Section (h), and the Commission should strike this
provision in its entirety.
        B.         The Commission Should Extend the Time Period to Sign an Interconnection
                   Agreement Under Subsection (f) to 60 to 90 Days.

        Under Section (f), a customer will have 30 days after completion of an interconnection
study to execute an interconnection agreement.8 A period of only 30 days to execute an
interconnection agreement, particularly one with the financial commitments proposed herein, is
not sufficient. CloudHQ understands that upon execution of the interconnection agreement,
additional study may be undertaken by ERCOT. Moreover, any delay in executing the
interconnection agreement may have downstream impacts on the ability of ERCOT to study other
interconnection requests. Thus, CloudHQ is sympathetic to the impacts that may occur from
adjusting the time for a party to execute an interconnection agreement following completion of the



        7
            Evaluation of Transmission Cost Recovery, Project No. 58484 (pending).
        8
            Proposed Interconnection Rules, Section (f), p. 18, lines 14-17.



                                                           5
 interconnection study. To balance the needs of businesses undertaking the investment to
interconnect against the impacts of a delay, CloudHQ respectfully requests a modest extension in
the time to sign an interconnection agreement upon completion of an interconnection study from
30 days to a more commercially reasonable period of 60 to 90 days.
           C.       The Commission Should Accept a Third-Party Guaranty.

           In Sections (d)(10)(C)(ii) and (d)(11)(C)(ii) applicable to the Intermediate Agreement and
in Sections (f)(8)(C)(ii) and (f)(10)(A)(ii) applicable to the Interconnection Agreement, the
Proposed Interconnection Rules authorize a customer to post financial security in the form of a
"corporate or parent guaranty, only if the corporation or parent corporation has a credit rating
equivalent of BBB-/Baa3 or higher from Standard & Poor's or Moody's." While the meaning of a
parental guaranty is straightforward, it is unclear what is meant by a "corporate guaranty." The
Commission should clarify the Proposed Interconnection Rules to confirm, or state expressly, that
a "corporate guaranty" includes a guaranty from a third-party, including a tenant of a data center.
From a policy perspective, the Commission should be agnostic to the source of the guaranty,
provided it is supported by appropriate credit ratings as set forth in the Proposed Interconnection
Rules and, where requested, "financial records or statements" that prove the guarantor's financial
ability.
           D.       The Financial Security Required by Sections (f)(7)-(10) of the Proposed
                    Interconnection Rules Appear Inconsistent with SB 6.

           There appears to be a disconnect between what SB 6 ordered the Commission to include
in the Proposed Interconnection Rules with respect to financial security versus what is presently
proposed in Sections (f)(7)-(10). Under SB 6, the Commission was directed to include as part of
these Proposed Interconnection Rules, "uniform financial commitment requirements for the
development of transmission infrastructure needed to serve a large load customer,"9 which SB 6
stated may include:
           (1) security provided on a dollar per megawatt basis as set by the commission;

           (2) contribution in aid of construction;




           9
               See PURA §37.0561(h)



                                                      6
          (3) security provided under an agreement that requires a large load customer to pay
             for significant equipment or services in advance of signing an agreement to
             establish electric delivery service; or

         (4) a form of financial commitment acceptable to the commission other than those
             provided by Subdivisions (1)-(3).10

Although the options for financial security permitted by SB 6 appear to only permit one form of
financial commitment (as denoted by the use of the word "or" between subsections (3) and (4) and
the option to propose "a" form other than those in (1)-(3)), the Proposed Interconnection Rules
have adopted an "and" approach, requiring a large load customer to supply four different, and
sometimes overlapping, forms of financial security.11 This raises a threshold question of whether
the Proposed Interconnection Rules are compliant with statute.
         As stated at the outset, CloudHQ fully supports a requirement that large load customers
must make up-front financial commitments as a pre-condition to interconnecting in the State. That
said, and practically speaking, it is unclear why all four forms of security are needed12 to ensure
customers are making sufficient up-front financial commitments.13 Moreover, it is not clear that
the four forms of security and payments proposed in the Proposed Interconnection Rules are
designed to recover discrete costs. To the contrary, it appears that a large load customer may be
paying overlapping financial security under the Proposed Interconnection Rules, essentially
paying 2-3 times for the same costs.
         For example, Subsection (f)(8) requires a customer to post financial security for
"equipment or services to interconnect the customer."14 Similarly, under Subsection (f)(9), the
customer must make a CIAC payment for "direct interconnection costs . . . costs associated with




         10
              Id. (emphasis added).
         11
              See Proposed Interconnection Rules, Sections (f)(7)-(10) at 1, lines 11-16.
          12
             The four forms of security required as part of executing the interconnection agreement stands in stark
contrast to the singular requirement under the intermediate agreement to post financial security equal to $50,000 per
MW. See Proposed Interconnection Rules, Section (d)(10).
         13
            Jurisdictions like the United Kingdom and France have looked beyond financial commitments to the utility
to ascertain whether a proposed request to interconnect is legitimate. For example, these jurisdictions have given
weight to a project having site control, local investment, rezoning, planning, and engineering and design in place.
While CloudHQ understands that proof of these elements is also required by the Proposed Interconnection Rules, see
Section (f)(1), (3), (4), CloudHQ would argue that having these elements is also proof that a project is not speculative.
         14
              Proposed Interconnection Rules at 23, lines 9-13.



                                                            7
 facilities built to interconnect the large load customer to the existing ERCOT system."15 Then,
under Subsection (f)(10), the customer must also "post financial security for system upgrades that
are necessary to reliably serve the large load customer."16 Each of these categories of financial
security seek to recover costs related to interconnection; there are no definitions or other clear
indications as to what costs to interconnect fall into which of these three buckets. Nor are there
any protections to ensure that customers will not have to post security or pay more than once for
the same cost. Finally, on top of these overlapping financial security and payment obligations,
Subsection (f)(7) inexplicably requires the customer to also pay a non-refundable fee equal to
$50,000 per MW of contracted peak demand, but the Proposed Interconnection Rules provide no
explanation as to what costs this fee covers, or why it would be needed in like of the three other
requirements to post financial security.
       From CloudHQ's perspective, determining whether SB 6 would permit the Commission to
impose multiple forms of financial security and payments is a threshold question the Commission
must answer. If the answer to this question is no, then the Proposed Interconnection Rules must be
amended to select the Commission's preferred form of financial security or payment. By contrast,
if the Commission believes that it may impose more than one type of financial security, then the
Proposed Interconnection Rules need to be amended to better explain how each form of financial
security and payments works and language needs to be added to ensure a customer does not need
to post double-security or double-pay for the same cost.
       E.         The Proposed Rules Regarding Refund are Inconsistent with the Language Set
                  Forth in PURA §37.0561(i).

       The Proposed Interconnection Rules provide a limited right of partial refund of monies
paid by a customer in one of three circumstances: (1) the customer withdraws all or a portion of
requested peak demand or contracted peak demand; (2) in the event there is non-utilized capacity;
or (3) the customer energizes. As discussed below, there are at least three problems with the refund
language in the Proposed Interconnection Rules.




       15
            Proposed Interconnection Rules at 25, lines 9-13.
       16
            Id. at 25, lines 21-23.



                                                         8
                     1.       The refund language in the proposed rules is inconsistent with SB 6.

         SB 6 states that security paid by a large load customer pursuant to (h)(1) ("security
provided on a dollar per megawatt basis") "must be refunded, in whole or in part, after the security
is applied to any outstanding amounts owed" under three circumstances:
         (1) as the large load customer meets the customer's load ramp milestones and
             sustains operations for a prescribed period as determined by the commission;

         (2) if the large load customer withdraws the customer's request for all or a portion
             of the requested capacity; or

         (3) if capacity subject to a financial commitment will be reallocated to one or more
             other customers.

(a "Refund Triggering Event")17

         Contrary to this unambiguous statutory language, the Proposed Interconnection Rules
make the $50,000 per MW fee almost entirely non-refundable at the intermediate agreement stage
and entirely non-refundable at the interconnection agreement stage.18 19 Because the Proposed
Interconnection Rules are contrary to statute, they must be amended.
                    2.       CloudHQ seeks clarification on the proposal to retain 80% of the
                             customer's financial security after all costs have been paid.

         Both SB 6 and the Proposed Interconnection Rules rightly require that, in the event of a
Refund Triggering Event, all costs incurred to interconnect the customer must be paid before any
amounts can be refunded to the customer.20 CloudHQ agrees that a large load customer should be
responsible for the costs they incur.
         At a macro level, CloudHQ sees wisdom, particularly during the intermediate agreement
phase, in there being to be some at-risk monies beyond the study fee to weed out speculative



         17
              Id. (emphasis added).
         18
            Also, missing from the Proposed Interconnection Rules is any explanation of where the $50,000 per MW
goes once it becomes non-refundable. By contrast, the Proposed Interconnection Rules are explicit that the other forms
of security subject to the 80% retention, see Section (g)(4), must be applied by the "TSP as an offset to the
interconnecting TSP's rate base." The Commission should ensure and clarify that any excess money, beyond cost
recovery for actual costs incurred, ultimately flows back for ratepayer benefit.
         19
              See Proposed Interconnection Rules, Sections (d)(10)(e), (f)(7), at 22, lines 20-22.
          20
             See PURA §37.0561(i); Proposed Interconnection Rules, Subsection (g)(2), at 27, lines 3-6; Subsection
(h)(2), at 28, line 9 to p. 29, line 2.



                                                            9
 interconnection requests in the queue.21 Reducing the number of purely speculative requests may
help spur business development in Texas as the remaining, likely more legitimate large load
interconnection requests, should be able to proceed through the queue and interconnect to the grid
in a timelier manner. That said, it is important that there be some rational and legitimate basis for
retaining customer deposits or financial security.
         The Proposed Interconnection Rules propose to limit the customer's refund to only
20 percent–with the DSP retaining 80 percent–after all costs have been paid and regardless of
whether the capacity is fully allocated to another customer.22 Keeping a portion of the financial
security for costs that are not incurred does not appear to follow traditional cost causation rate-
making principles. While, as discussed above, CloudHQ is generally supportive of some at-risk
monies beyond the study fee to weed out speculative interconnection requests in the queue, it is
critical to strike the appropriate balance between weeding out such speculative requests and not
overly limiting real business development within Texas. To that end, CloudHQ believes that the
Commission must provide a legitimate jurisdiction for–or make appropriate adjustments to–the
80/20 proposal set forth in the Proposed Interconnection Rules.
                    3.       If capacity or peak demand is reallocated, there is no reason to keep or
                             draw down or retain a customer's financial security.

         PURA § 37.0561(i) also expressly authorizes a customer refund "if capacity subject to a
financial commitment will be reallocated to one or more other customers." Two sections of the
Proposed Interconnection Rules state that ERCOT "must reallocate non-utilized capacity," but
they make no mention of any refund as a direct result of reallocating the capacity.23 24 Yet again,


         21
            See Proposed Interconnection Rules, Sections 10(E) and (g)(3)(4) (indicating that the customer would
receive at most $10,000 per MW, i.e., 20 percent of $50,000 per MW as a refund if it were to reduce its capacity or
withdrawal its capacity request during the intermediate agreement phrase).
         22
              See Proposed Rules, Section (g)(4) and (h)(4).
         23
            Section (h)(1) of the Proposed Reallocation Rules also obligate ERCOT to reallocate capacity if a customer
fails to meet a milestone during phased energization by six months. As discussed in Section III(A) of these comments,
Section (h)(1) of the Proposed Interconnection Rules and the automatic reallocation of capacity contained therein
should be struck in its entirety. Despite Cloud HQ's objections to Section (h)(1), it is worth noting that the Proposed
Interconnection Rules are silent as to what happens from a refund perspective if an automatic reallocation were to
occur under Section (h)(1). A loss of capacity forced upon a customer falls squarely within PURA § 37.0561(i)(3),
which requires the customer to be refunded if "capacity subject to a financial commitment will be reallocated to one
or more other customers." Despite this clear directive in the law, there is no mention of any refund if capacity is
reallocated against a customer's will under Section (h)(1) of the Proposed Interconnection Rules.
         24
              See Proposed Interconnection Rules, Subsection (g)(6) and (h)(6).



                                                          10
 this appears to be an area where the Proposed Interconnection Rules are inconsistent with its
enacting legislation.
         CloudHQ does acknowledge–as does SB 6–that there may be situations when a large load
customer has a legitimate reason to voluntarily withdrawal its capacity request, reduce its capacity
needs or wishes to release allocated capacity that is unutilized. Under such voluntary conditions,
it is beneficial to all customers that such capacity be reallocated.25 If and when this happens, it
does not make sense to penalize a customer by either drawing down their financial security or
retaining their financial security, beyond (i) applying that financial security to cover costs that
were incurred solely to interconnect the customer and that will not be recovered via the reallocated
capacity, and (ii) retaining the at-risk monies to weed out speculative interconnection requests as
discussed above. If ERCOT successfully reallocates capacity or peak demand, then that means that
another customer is taking on the financial responsibility for that capacity or demand. As such,
retaining or drawing down the original customer's financial security and payments would be both
punitive and result in double recovery for the same costs. The Proposed Interconnection Rules
should be amended to incorporate procedures for determining how a customer's financial security
and payments will be fully refunded in the event that ERCOT successfully reallocates capacity
and demand.
IV.     CONCLUSION

         CloudHQ understands the immense pressures facing Texas and supports commonsense
measures designed to protect against speculative large load growth. At the same time, CloudHQ
is concerned that the Proposed Interconnection Rules go too far in their efforts to avoid stranded
costs and will have the unintended effect of stifling business development in the State in a manner
contrary to the will of the legislature as expressed in SB 6. CloudHQ greatly appreciates the
opportunity to provide these Comments for Commission consideration and respectfully requests
that the Commission implement the proposed revisions set forth herein.




         25
            With the financial security requirements that are likely to be adopted via this proceeding as well as the
minimum demand charges being contemplated by Project No. 58484, Cloud HQ expects instances of under-utilized
capacity to be infrequent.

                                       PROJECT NO. 58481

RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                            §               BEFORE THE
LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                         §       PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
STANDARDS UNDER PURA 37.0561                       §                OF TEXAS

              EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF CLOUDHQ, LLC'S COMMENTS

   Sections (h)(1), (6) of the Proposed Interconnection Rules should be stricken in their entirety
    because they are unjust, unreasonable, vague, unnecessary, and fail to achieve the balance
    mandated by SB 6.

       Section (h)'s removal of capacity from a customer that has already connected to the grid
        and put forward substantial capital, sometimes billions of dollars, to do so is unjustly and
        unreasonably punitive.

       Section (h)(1) is also vague since "milestone" is undefined.

       Section (h)(1) gives TSPs and DSPs the unilateral right to determine that a milestone has
        been missed triggering capacity reallocation without giving affected customers a dispute
        resolution process to contest such a determination.

       Section (h)(1) is unnecessary as there are other, more appropriate customer protections
        available to minimize the risk of stranded costs, including the financial security required
        under the Proposed Interconnection Rules, some of which is non-refundable, and the
        minimum demand charges currently being considered in Project No. 58484.

   The Commission should extend the time period to sign an interconnection agreement under
    Section (f) of the Proposed Interconnection Rules from 30 days to a more commercially
    reasonable period of 60 to 90 days.

   The Commission should confirm that the "corporate guaranty" authorized by
    Sections (d)(10)(C)(ii) and (d)(11)(C)(ii) (Intermediate Agreement) and Sections (f)(8)(C)(ii)
    and (f)(10)(A)(ii) (Interconnection Agreement) includes third-party guarantees.

   Sections (f)(7)-(10) of the Proposed Interconnection Rules should be amended to be consistent
    with SB 6 by only requiring one form of financial security.

   Sections (d)(10)(E) and (f)(7) of the Proposed Interconnection Rules should be amended to
    align with SB 6's statutory requirement that the security provided on a dollar per megawatt
    basis must be refundable after payment of all costs.

   The Commission should justify the proposal in Sections (g)(3)-(4) and (h)(3)-(4) of the
    Proposed Interconnection Rules that a TSP or DSP keep 80 percent of customer's financial
    security, or, if such a justification does not exist, the Commission should propose an
    appropriate customer refund amount.



                                                12
    It does not make sense for a TSP or DSP to retain a customer's financial security if the capacity
    is successfully reallocated. The Proposed Interconnection Rules should be amended to
    incorporate procedures for determining how a customer's financial security and payments will
    be refunded after costs are paid in the event that ERCOT successfully reallocates capacity and
    demand as provided in Sections (g)(6) and (h)(6).



                                                      Respectfully submitted,

                                                      /s/ Mike Benn
                                                      Mike Benn
                                                      VP Energy Strategy & Procurement




Dated: April 17, 2026

                                 CLOUDHO,LLC'S COMMENTS

        On March 16, 2026, the Public Utility Commission of Texas ("PUCT" or "Commission")
published its " (Staff Recommendation) Proposal for Publication" relating to Large Load
Interconnection Standards, 16 Texas Administrative Code (TAC) § 25.194 (the "Proposed
Interconnection Rules"), as mandated by Public Utility Regulatory Act (PURA) § 37.0561,
enacted by Senate Bill (SB) 6 during the Texas 89th Regular Legislative Session ("SB 6"). In
publishing the Proposed Interconnection Rules, the Commission specifically requested comments
on the proposed rules, including "the costs associated with, and benefits that will be gained by,
implementation of the proposed rule." In response to the Commission's request for comments,
CloudHQ LLC ("CloudHQ") herein provides its comments and proposed revisions to the Proposed
Interconnection Rules.
I.      ABOUT CLOUDHQ

        CloudHQ1 is global data center company that partners with the world's largest technology
companies to provide reliable and secure power and operating infrastructure. Since its founding in
2016, CloudHQ and its affiliates have successfully leased data centers totaling 1,380 megawatts
("MWs") of capacity across 24 campuses around the globe, with proj ects in the United States,
United Kingdom, European Union, Asia-Pacific, Central America, and South America. Presently,
CloudHQ is actively pursuing the development of an additional 5 GW of capacity across the globe,
including a -500 MW data center that it is currently developing west of San Antonio on the former
University of Texas Health Science Center site.2
        This background is provided so that the Commission understands that CloudHQ's interest

II.    INTRODUCTION

       With an ERCOT interconnection queue that has ballooned to 410 GW as of April 1,2026,3
CloudHQ recognizes-and strongly supports the conclusion-that something must be done to ensure
that (1) the load seeking interconnection is real and not speculative; and (2) that any new load pays
its fair share. CloudHQ is fully supportive of requiring large load customers to make up-front
financial commitments as a pre-condition to interconnecting in the State. At the same time,
interconnecting should not become so onerous, expensive, and punitive that it disincentivizes (if
not eviscerates) large load investment and business development in the State.
       Fundamentally, CloudHQ believes that SB 6 properly sought to address the problems
facing ERCOT without stopping alllarge load growth in Texas. Unlike SB 6, however, CloudHQ
does not believe that the Proposed Interconnection Rules adequately balance these interests,
however, it is critical that this balance is reflected in the final version of these rules because SB 6
demands it. Specifically, SB 6 obligates the Commission to
       establish standards for interconnecting large load customers in the ERCOT power
       region in a manner designed to support business development in this state while
       minimizing the potential for stranded infrastructure costs and maintaining system
       reliability.4

The Commission was directed to establish interconnection rules that are designed to support
business development while mitigating the risks of stranded costs and maintaining system
reliability. The Proposed Interconnection Rules fail to achieve the balance explicitly set forth in
SB 6. As written, the Proposed Interconnection Rules focus solely on eliminating (rather than
mitigating) customer risk, and rather than taking steps to ensure that business development will be
supported, they instead go the opposite direction, unduly restricting future large, grid connected,
load. Without changes, the Proposed Interconnection Rules have the potential to significantly stifle
business development and growth in Texas.

 III.    COMMENTS

       A.       The Commission Should Strike Section (h) from the Final Rule.

       From CloudHQ's perspective, the single most problematic provision of the Proposed
Interconnection Rules is set forth in Section (h)(1), (6) where it states in relevant part:
       Not later than 30 days after a large load customer fails, by 6 months, to satisfy a
       milestone in its schedule for phased energization, the interconnecting DSP or the
       interconnecting TSP must noti fy ERCOT of the large load customer's non-utilized
       capacity ... [andl ERCOT must reallocate non-utilized capacity.5

This provision is unjust, unreasonable, vague, and unnecessary, and it should be stricken from the
Proposed Interconnection Rules in its entirety.
        The fundamental problem currently facing the Texas grid is not whether interconnected
load will use power once interconnected and operational. The real problems are in (1) determining
how much of the 410 GW in the queue is real and (2) in interconnecting such load, ensuring that
this new load-rather than existing customers-pay for the costs they cause. In proposing to take
away capacity from a customer that has already connected to the grid and paid substantial costs to
be interconnected, Section (h)(1) unjustly and unreasonably punishes large loads who legitimately
want to do business in Texas while not solving the fundamental issues facing the Texas grid.
       Not only is Section (h) unnecessary, but it unfairly vague. It is unclear what "milestone"
means within the context of Section (h) as it is undefined. Further, while Section (h)(1) discusses
a "large load customer" who "fails...to satisfy a milestone," there is no explanation of how to
determine whether a failed milestone is material, let alone whether the missed milestone is the
customer's fault as opposed to the fault of the transmission service provider ("TSP"), the
distribution service provider ("DSP"), ERCOT, or some other party.
        Section (h)(1) is also fundamentally unfair. While a TSP and DSP appear to be given carte
blanche to unilaterally determine that a milestone has been missed by a customer, there is no
process in place for a customer to challenge a determination by a TSP or DSP that a customer
failure has occurred so as to trigger ERCOT's reallocation of the capacity. Quite simply,
Section (h) of the Proposed Interconnection Rules could leave a customer who has expended
millions, if not billions of dollars, in capital, at risk of losing contracted-and paid-for capacity

deploy approximately $2 billion of capital to construct a data center proj ect, not including land

milestone in its schedule for phased energization by six months and one day, the large load

fabrication facilities, or other large industrial customers could bear. The consequences of this

SB 6, but it may also significantly stifle future business expansion and large-scale, grid-

           C.     The Commission Should Accept a Third-Party Guaranty.

           In Sections (d)(10)(C)(ii) and (d)(11)(C)(ii) applicable to the Intermediate Agreement and
in Sections (f)(8)(C)(ii) and (f)(10)(A)(ii) applicable to the Interconnection Agreement, the
Proposed Interconnection Rules authorize a customer to post financial security in the form of a
"corporate or parent guaranty, only if the corporation or parent corporation has a credit rating
equivalent of BBB-/Baa3 or higher from Standard & Poor's or Moody's." While the meaning of a
parental guaranty is straightforward, it is unclear what is meant by a "corporate guaranty." The
Commission should clarify the Proposed Interconnection Rules to confirm, or state expressly, that
a "corporate guaranty" includes a guaranty from a third-party, including a tenant of a data center.
From a policy perspective, the Commission should be agnostic to the source of the guaranty,
provided it is supported by appropriate credit ratings as set forth in the Proposed Interconnection
Rules and, where requested, "financial records or statements" that prove the guarantor's financial
ability.

IV.      CONCLUSION

         CloudHQ understands the immense pressures facing Texas and supports commonsense
measures designed to protect against speculative large load growth. At the same time, CloudHQ
is concerned that the Proposed Interconnection Rules go too far in their efforts to avoid stranded
costs and will have the unintended effect of stifling business development in the State in a manner
contrary to the will of the legislature as expressed in SB 6. CloudHQ greatly appreciates the
opportunity to provide these Comments for Commission consideration and respectfully requests
that the Commission implement the proposed revisions set forth herein.
